extraction_text: Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya who will initiate the battle between the Kauravas and the Pandavas.
Sanjaya reports that Duryodhana, with his brothers, positions Bhishma at the forefront to lead the Kaurava army forward.

relationships: Commander (Bhishma) leading the Kaurava army under Duryodhana's orders

extraction_text: The Pandava army, with Bhima as their vanguard, advances joyfully, eager to engage Bhishma.

relationships: Bhima as the Pandava vanguard opposing Bhishma

extraction_text: Both armies clash with immense noise from conches, drums, war cries, horses, and elephants, creating a tumultuous scene.

supernatural_elements: The clamor is compared to a storm shaking a forest and stirring the ocean

extraction_text: Bhima roars mightily, overpowering all battle sounds and causing Duryodhana's troops to tremble and their mounts to excrete in fear.

relationships: Bhima's roar demoralizes the Kaurava forces

extraction_text: Duryodhana and his brothers, along with allies like Vikarna, Duhshasana, and Bhagadatta, surround Bhima and shower him with arrows.

relationships: Kaurava princes and allies jointly target Bhima

extraction_text: The sons of Draupadi, Abhimanyu, Nakula, Sahadeva, and Shikhandi counter-attack Duryodhana and his brothers with arrows.

relationships: Pandava allies engage the Kaurava princes in combat

extraction_text: The battle intensifies with skilled archers from both sides, including Drona's disciples, exchanging fierce arrow volleys, while other kings watch as spectators.

relationships: Drona's trained warriors participate actively; neutral kings observe

extraction_text: Emotionally charged warriors from both sides, bearing old grudges, challenge each other to duels amidst the chaotic battlefield.
On Duryodhana's command, all the kings and their armies charge forward with bows ready, fully engaging in the battle.

relationships: Duryodhana orders the final, all-out assault

extraction_text: Yudhishthira commanded thousands of kings to charge at the Kaurava army led by Duryodhana.

attributes.relationship: Cousins and rivals in the Kurukshetra War

extraction_text: The armies of the Kauravas and Pandavas engaged in fierce combat, creating dust that obscured the sun.
Bhishma's brilliance outshone all armies in the terrifying chaos of battle.

attributes.relationship: Grandsire of both Kauravas and Pandavas

extraction_text: On the morning of a terrifying day, the Kurukshetra War continued with slaughter of kings' bodies.
Bhishma personally charged at Arjuna in battle, wielding a terrible bow like the rod of Time.
Arjuna charged at Bhishma, who was at the forefront, wielding his famous Gandiva bow.

attributes.relationship: Mutual attempt to kill each other

extraction_text: Bhishma and Arjuna exchanged attacks but neither could overcome the other.
Satyaki charged at Shalya, and they engaged in a hair-raising mixed battle.
Satyaki and Shalya shot terrible arrows at each other, both becoming covered in arrows like flowering Kinshuka trees.
Abhimanyu fought with Brihadbala, who cut Abhimanyu's flag and struck down his charioteer.
Enraged at his charioteer's fall, Abhimanyu shot nine arrows at Brihadbala.
Abhimanyu shot crescent-headed arrows at Brihadbala, cutting his flag, front axle, and striking down his charioteer.
Bhima fought with Duryodhana on the battlefield.
Bhima and Duryodhana, both great warriors and tigers among men, showered each other with arrows.
All beings were amazed watching Bhima and Duryodhana, both great-souled and skilled warriors.
Dushasana charged at the great warrior Nakula, shooting many deadly arrows at him.
Madri's son Nakula shot arrows, cutting off his opponent's banner and bow, then shot twenty-five small-headed arrows.
Duryodhana (your son) struck down his opponent's chariot pole and banner with arrows in the great battle.
Krishna (Krishna) charged toward Sahadeva in battle and showered him with arrows.
Sahadeva struck down Krishna's charioteer with extremely sharp arrows.
Yudhishthira personally charged toward Shalya, and Shalya broke Yudhishthira's bow in half.
Yudhishthira discarded the broken bow and took up another more powerful bow, then covered Shalya with straight arrows, saying 'Wait, wait!'
Dhrishtadyumna charged toward Drona, and Drona angrily broke Dhrishtadyumna's deadly bow into three pieces.
Drona shot an extremely terrible arrow that struck Dhrishtadyumna's body, then Dhrishtadyumna took up another bow and fourteen arrows to counterattack Drona.

attributes.relationship: Fierce battle between commander and disciple

extraction_text: Shalya charged toward Vrishasena in the battlefield, saying 'Wait, wait!'
Shalya struck Vrishasena's right arm, and Vrishasena struck Shalya's collarbone.
Yudhamanyu charged toward Pulika in battle with great anger.
Pulika roared like a lion and shot many arrows at Yudhamanyu, then Yudhamanyu quickly shot nine arrows at Pulika.
Ghatotkacha charged toward the rakshasa Alambusha in battle.
Ghatotkacha shot ninety sharp arrows at Alambusha, and Alambusha shot straight arrows at Ghatotkacha in return.
Shikhandi charged toward Ashwatthama in battle, and Ashwatthama shot extremely sharp iron arrows that made Shikhandi tremble.
Shikhandi counterattacked Ashwatthama with sharp sandalwood arrows.
Virata charged toward Bhurishrava and began fighting.
Viraata was struck by Bhurishravas and became furious, showering arrows like a cloud raining on a mountain.
Bhurishravas quickly covered King Viraata with arrows like a cloud covering the rising sun.
Kripa, son of Sharadvata, charged at King Shrutayu of Kekaya and covered him with arrows.
Shrutayu and Kripa exchanged arrow showers, killed each other's horses, and broke each other's bows.
Shrutayu and Kripa, having lost their chariots, approached each other angrily and fought with swords.
Drupada, filled with joy, charged at the cheerful King Jayadratha of Sindhu.
Jayadratha shot three arrows at Drupada, who retaliated in battle.
Vikarna, your son, charged at the mighty Shikhandin with fast horses and began fighting.
Vikarna shot many arrows but could not shake Shikhandin, and Shikhandin could not shake Vikarna either.
The great warrior Kuntibhoja, filled with anger for the benefit of the Pandavas, bravely charged at the tiger among men, Shalya.
Shalya covered the great warrior Kuntibhoja with a vast shower of arrows in battle.
Kuntibhoja, emotionally stirred, covered Shalya with many arrows like a cloud covering a mountain.
The heroic Shakuni charged at the heroic Uttara, like one mad elephant charging at another.
Uttara, son of Yudhishthira, filled with anger, shot many sharp arrows at Shakuni, son of Subala, like Indra attacking the Danavas.
The wise Shakuni retaliated against Uttara, shooting many straight arrows at him.
Shrutakarman charged at the heroic Shikhandin of the Kambojas in battle.
Shikhandin attacked the great warrior Shrutakarman, son of Sahadeva, but could not shake him, like not being able to shake Mount Mainaka.
The angry Shrutakarman shot many arrows at the Kamboja hero Shikhandin, as if hitting his entire body.
Iravan, filled with anger, charged at the indignant Alambusha in battle, each more valiant than the other.
The great warrior Iravan, son of Arjuna, killed Alambusha's horse in battle and let out a great roar, pleasing the soldiers.
Alambusha, filled with anger, also killed Iravan's horse with a mace in battle, then continued fighting.
Anuvinda and Vinda of Avanti engaged in battle with the great warrior Kuntibhoja, who was leading his sons and army.
Anuvinda struck Kuntibhoja with a club, and Kuntibhoja quickly shot a large number of arrows.
Kuntibhoja's son also shot arrows at Vinda, who retaliated.
The five brothers of Kekaya and the five princes of Gandhara, each leading armies, clashed on the battlefield.
Your son Duryodhana fought with the excellent warrior Uttara, son of Viraata, shooting many sharp arrows at him.
Uttara shot many sharp arrows at the warrior.
King of Chedi charged at Uluka in battle.
Uluka shot many sharp feathered arrows at the King of Chedi.
The two invincible warriors fought each other furiously in a terrible scene.
Both sides engaged in thousands of paired combats with chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry.
The battle appeared magnificent at first glance but quickly became chaotic and indiscernible.
Elephants charged elephants, charioteers charged charioteers, horses charged horses, and infantry charged infantry.
Warriors attacked each other fiercely on the battlefield in intense, deadlocked combat.
Gods, sages, Siddhas, and Charanas gathered to watch this terrible war resembling the battle between gods and asuras.
Thousands of elephants and chariots, streams of horses and men, broke from their formations.
Chariots, elephants, infantry, and cavalry were seen everywhere repeatedly engaging in combat.
Sanjaya described hundreds and thousands of chaotic battles occurring here and there, then and now.
Sons did not recognize fathers, fathers did not recognize sons, brothers did not recognize brothers, uncles did not recognize nephews.
Nephews did not recognize uncles, friends did not recognize friends as Pandavas and Kauravas fought as if possessed by demons.
Some tiger-like men overturned chariot formations with chariot formations, broke chariot yokes with chariot yokes.
Some broke chariot poles with chariot poles, broke axles with axles, all eager to kill each other.
Some chariots were blocked by other chariots and could not advance.
Some large elephants with split temples were blocked by other elephants.
Some angry elephants with lances and banners repeatedly attacked other elephants with their tusks.
Some elephants were wounded by tusks of other fierce elephants, suffering and crying out in pain.
Some well-trained elephants with split temples, driven by goads and hooks, charged other elephants with split temples.
Some elephants entangled with other elephants with split temples, chasing and running while making heron-like cries.
Some excellent trained elephants with split temples were struck by swords, lances, and iron arrows.
Struck in vital spots, they fell down dead crying, while other elephants fled everywhere with terrible roars.

Warriors protecting elephant legs, broad-chested and equipped with swords, bows, bright battle-axes, clubs, maces, javelins, lances, iron bolts, and bright sharp swords, were seen running everywhere eager to kill each other.
Warriors were seen attacking each other with bright swords dripping with human blood.
Heroes' arms swung swords cutting and striking fatal spots while emitting sharp cries.
The battle involves various combat methods including bludgeoning with clubs, slashing with swords, goring with tusks, and trampling by elephants.
Cavalry on swift horses attack each other, with some jumping onto chariots to behead charioteers.
Charioteers retaliate by shooting arrows to kill cavalry within range.
Elephants decorated with gold trample horses and riders, while some elephants are wounded by spears.
Spears and javelins fly like snakes, piercing warriors and armor.

extraction_text: Some Kshatriya warriors continue fighting joyfully, cursing enemies without surrendering.
Heroic warriors endure arrow wounds silently or request to board other chariots after losing theirs.
Fathers kill sons, sons kill fathers, nephews kill maternal uncles, and maternal uncles kill nephews.
